usage: to move away (to a new place)
이사 가다 stresses leaving toward a destination; pairs with 로/으로 for where you go
Use 오다 when the new place is near the speaker: 옆집에 이사 왔어요 'someone moved in next door'
이삿짐 = moving load; 싸다 'to pack/wrap', the standard verb for boxing up belongings
잡다 here means 'to fix/secure' a date, a very common collocation for scheduling
examples: 저 다음 달에 이사해요.
I'm moving next month.
Bare 이사해요 already implies changing homes; no extra object needed
집이 좁아서 더 넓은 곳으로 이사하고 싶어요.
The house is cramped, so I want to move somewhere bigger.
Destination 'somewhere bigger' takes 으로, the direction particle
이번 주말에 이사하는데 좀 도와줄 수 있어요?
I'm moving this weekend, could you help out a bit?
-는데 sets up the situation before the request — natural spoken framing
nuance: 이사하다 specifically means relocating your residence — changing the home you live in — built from Sino-Korean 移徙 (移 'shift', 徙 'relocate') plus 하다. Contrast it sharply with 옮기다, which is just physically moving an object from one spot to another (책상을 옮기다 'move the desk'); you never use 옮기다 for changing homes, and you never use 이사하다 for shifting furniture. It splits into 이사 가다 (move away, focus on departure) and 이사 오다 (move in, focus on arrival near the speaker). Being a 하다-verb, the negative wraps the noun: 이사 안 해요 / 이사 못 해요, NOT 안 이사해요. The biggest English-speaker pitfall is treating it like English 'move' as a transitive verb — Koreans don't say '집을 이사해요'; the home is implied, so just 이사해요 is complete.

Saying 집을 이사해요 by direct-translating 'move house' — 이사하다 already contains the idea of home, so the object is dropped; just say 이사해요.
Using 옮기다 for relocating yourself (e.g. 서울로 옮겼어요) — 옮기다 is only for moving objects; for changing residence use 서울로 이사했어요.

usage: Object takes 를; the lent thing is the direct object
The recipient takes 에게 (written) or 한테 (spoken): 친구한테 빌려줬어요
잠깐 'briefly' softens the ask, very common with small items like a pen or phone
흔쾌히 'readily, with no hesitation' — describes a generous lender
examples: 펜 좀 빌려줘.
Lend me a pen.
Casual 줘 + 좀 = the everyday way friends ask to borrow something
제 우산을 빌려줄까요?
Shall I lend you my umbrella?
-ㄹ까요 offers your own action; you're proposing to do the lending
지금 현금이 없어서 빌려줄 수가 없어요.
I have no cash right now, so I just can't lend you any.
-ㄹ 수가 없다 with 가 adds an apologetic 'really can't' nuance
nuance: 빌려주다 is literally 빌려 (lend-and) + 주다 (give), so it means 'borrow-out to someone' — you give something for temporary use, expecting it back. The crucial contrast is with 빌리다, which is the SAME root from the other direction: 빌리다 = to borrow (you receive), 빌려주다 = to lend (you give). English speakers constantly swap these because casual English even uses 'borrow me your pen', but Korean keeps them strictly separate — 친구에게 책을 빌려줬어요 'I lent a book to my friend' vs 친구에게서 책을 빌렸어요 'I borrowed a book from my friend'. Watch the particles: the thing takes 를, the person you lend TO takes 에게/한테, whereas with 빌리다 the person you borrow FROM takes 에게서/한테서. The 주다 ending also carries a giving/favor feeling, so 빌려주다 sounds kind and helpful, which is why polite requests are simply 빌려주세요.

mistakes: Confusing direction: saying 친구한테 책을 빌렸어요 when you mean you GAVE the book — to lend you must use 빌려줬어요. 빌리다 = receive, 빌려주다 = give.
Marking the recipient with the wrong particle: with 빌려주다 the person takes 에게/한테 (to whom), not 에게서/한테서 (from whom, which belongs to 빌리다).
Dropping the 주다 and just saying 빌려요 to mean 'I lend' — 빌리다 by itself means 'borrow', so 'lend' needs the full 빌려주다.

usage: The most basic collocation; 쓰레기 'garbage' is the prototypical object
Korea separates trash strictly; 분리수거 is the sorted-disposal counterpart to plain 버리다
As an auxiliary, 버리다 adds 'all gone': 다 먹어 버렸어요 'I ate it all up'
미련 없이 'with no lingering attachment' — common when decluttering
examples: 이거 버려도 돼요?
Is it okay to throw this away?
-아도 돼요 asks permission before discarding something
안 입는 옷은 다 버렸어요.
I threw out all the clothes I don't wear.
Topic 옷은 sets 'as for clothes'; 다 'all' shows total disposal
아직 쓸 만하니까 버리지 마세요.
It's still usable, so please don't throw it away.
-ㄹ 만하다 'worth doing' justifies keeping it
nuance: 버리다 means to discard something as no longer wanted — to throw it out as trash or to abandon it. Don't confuse it with 던지다, which is to throw an object through the air toward a target (공을 던지다 'throw a ball'); 버리다 is about getting rid of, not about the flying motion. A second hugely important use is as an auxiliary verb -아/어 버리다, which colors the main verb with 'completely' or 'regrettably/finally': 잊어버리다 'forget (clean out of mind)', 가 버리다 '(someone) just left'. So a learner must read context: 버려요 alone = throw away, but 먹어 버려요 = eat it all up. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 던지다 whenever they see 'throw' — but 'throw away/out' in the disposal sense is always 버리다. Also note Korea's strict 분리수거 (recycling separation) culture, so 버리다 in daily life often pairs with sorting.

Forgetting that 버리다 also means 'abandon (a person)' (애인을 버리다) — so in emotional contexts it can sound harsh; don't use it lightly about people.

usage: Object takes 를; common in volunteer/clean-up contexts
to pick up off the floor
The place you pick it up from takes 에서, not 에
to pick up and gather (back in)
주워 담다 = scoop fallen things back into a container; also figurative for 'take back words'
to find/pick up on the street
Colloquially 'where did you pick that up?' implies finding something for free
examples: 저거 좀 주워 줘.
Pick that up for me.
Casual 주워 줘 = pick up as a favor; the irregular form 주워 in action
바닥에 떨어진 동전을 주웠어요.
I picked up a coin that fell on the floor.
Place 바닥에 + 떨어진 'fallen' set the scene; past 주웠어요 shows ㅂ→우
허리가 아파서 못 주워요.
My back hurts, so I can't pick it up.
Inability 못 + irregular 주워요; bending down is the implied difficulty
nuance: 줍다 means to pick up something that is lying on the ground or floor, usually by bending down — typically things that fell or litter. It contrasts with 들다 'to lift/hold up' (which is about raising weight, no fallen-object implication) and with 집다 'to grab/pinch with fingers' (a precise small grasp, e.g. with chopsticks). Crucially 줍다 is a ㅂ-irregular verb: before a vowel ending the ㅂ turns into a 우 sound, giving 주워, 주워요, 주웠어요, 주울 거예요 — but before a consonant ending the ㅂ stays, so the formal style is 줍습니다 (not 주웁니다) and 'don't' is 줍지 마세요. The classic English-speaker pitfall is regularizing it to 줍어요; that is wrong — say 주워요. Also note the place you pick it up FROM takes 에서 (바닥에서 주웠어요), since picking up is an action happening at a location.

Over-applying the irregular to consonant endings: saying 주웁니다 — before the consonant ㅅ the ㅂ is kept, so formal is 줍습니다.
Using 들다 (lift) for something on the floor: 바닥에서 동전을 들었어요 sounds off; for retrieving a fallen item use 줍다 → 주웠어요.

usage: Object takes 를; brittle items (glass, dishes, eggs) are typical objects
Same verb, different sense: 잠을 깨다 'snap out of sleep'; 잠이 깨다 = sleep breaks (intransitive)
Figurative 'shatter' a record; also 침묵을 깨다 'break the silence'
깨뜨리다 stresses the actor caused the breakage, slightly stronger than plain 깨다
examples: 컵 깰까 봐 조심했어요.
I was careful in case I'd break the cup.
-ㄹ까 봐 'fearing that' — worrying about breaking it
계란을 깨서 그릇에 넣으세요.
Crack the eggs and put them in the bowl.
Cooking: 깨다 also covers cracking an eggshell open
이거 비싼 거니까 깨지 마세요.
This is expensive, so please don't break it.
-지 마세요 prohibition; 깨다 is transitive (you break it)
nuance: 깨다 (transitive) means to break a hard, brittle thing into pieces — glass, dishes, eggs — by impact. Distinguish it from 부수다, which is to smash/demolish a larger or sturdier structure (벽을 부수다 'break down a wall'), and from 깨지다, the intransitive partner: 내가 컵을 깼어요 'I broke the cup (I did it)' vs 컵이 깨졌어요 'the cup broke (it got broken)'. The same syllable 깨다 also means to wake up from sleep (잠을 깨다 / 잠에서 깨다), and figuratively to 'break' a record, silence, or atmosphere — so context decides. The English-speaker pitfall is using 깨다 for things that don't shatter: tearing paper is 찢다, snapping a stick is 부러뜨리다, and breaking a machine so it stops working is 고장 내다 — not 깨다. Conjugation is regular: stem 깨- + 어 contracts to 깨, past 깼어요.

Using 깨다 for non-brittle breakage: 종이를 깼어요 for tearing paper is wrong — tearing is 찢다; a snapped stick is 부러뜨리다.
Saying 고장났어요 vs 깼어요 mix-up: a broken-down phone is 고장 났어요 (stopped working), not 깼어요, which implies you physically shattered it.

usage: to spill water / let water drip
Object takes 를; small amounts dribbling out, often onto clothes
흘리다 is the standard verb for crying tears running down — 눈물을 흘리다
땀을 흘리다 'let sweat drip' — the normal way to say someone is sweating
to drop bits of food while eating
Common gentle scold to kids: spilling crumbs/rice as you eat
examples: 국 흘리지 않게 조심해.
Be careful not to spill the soup.
-지 않게 'so as not to' + casual warning
아이가 밥을 자꾸 흘려요.
The kid keeps dropping rice (while eating).
자꾸 'repeatedly' + 흘려요; eating-spill sense
감동해서 눈물을 흘렸어요.
I was so moved that I shed tears.
Idiomatic 눈물을 흘리다 for crying; past 흘렸어요
nuance: 흘리다 is the transitive 'cause to flow/drip' — to let liquid or small grains escape and run out, usually a little at a time and by accident (옷에 국을 흘렸어요 'I dribbled soup on my clothes'). Two big contrasts: first, its intransitive partner is 흐르다 'to flow' (물이 흐르다 'water flows by itself') — don't say 흘러요 when YOU spilled it; you need 흘려요. Second, against 쏟다: 쏟다 is dumping a large amount out all at once (a whole cup tipping over), while 흘리다 is a gentler, trickling spill. Beyond liquids, 흘리다 is the idiomatic verb for bodily flow — 눈물을 흘리다 'shed tears', 땀을 흘리다 'sweat', 피를 흘리다 'bleed'. The English-speaker pitfall is the 흐르다/흘리다 confusion: English 'spill' is transitive, so map it to 흘리다 (or 쏟다 for big spills), never 흐르다.

Using 흘리다 for a big sudden spill: knocking over a full glass is better said 쏟다 (쏟았어요) — 흘리다 implies a small, dribbling amount.
Forgetting the body-fluid idioms: trying to say 'cry' with 울다 only — to describe tears running down, Koreans say 눈물을 흘리다, and 땀을 흘리다 for sweating.

usage: 묶다 is the go-to verb for tying hair into a ponytail; object 를
The binding material takes 으로 (means): 끈으로 묶어요
묶다 = make the knot; the opposite (loosen) is 풀다
하나로 'into one' — group several things together with a tie or, figuratively, combine them
examples: 머리 좀 묶어 줄까?
Want me to tie your hair up?
Casual offer -아 줄까; everyday between friends/family
박스를 끈으로 단단히 묶었어요.
I tied the box up tightly with string.
단단히 'firmly' + means 끈으로; past 묶었어요
택배 보내게 이 상자 좀 묶어 주세요.
Please tie up this box so I can ship it.
-게 'so that' links purpose to the request
nuance: 묶다 means to tie or bind things together with string, rope, or a band so they stay fastened — boxes, hair, shoelaces, bundles. Its natural antonym is 풀다 'to untie/undo'. Distinguish it from 매다, which specifically means to fasten by knotting around something (넥타이를 매다 'tie a necktie', 안전벨트를 매다 'fasten a seatbelt') — 매다 is about securing a band to/around the body, while 묶다 is the general 'bind together' for objects and hair. Note the binding material takes 으로: 끈으로 묶다 'tie with string'. Pronunciation is a trap: the ㄲ batchim before a vowel links, so 묶어요 sounds like [무꺼요], but you must spell it 묶어요, and the formal form is 묶습니다 [묵씀니다]. The English-speaker pitfall is reaching for 매다 for everything 'tie' — but for hair, boxes, and bundles, the correct verb is 묶다.

Forgetting the means particle: saying 끈을 묶어요 to mean 'tie WITH string' — the tool takes 으로, so it is 끈으로 묶어요 (끈을 묶어요 would mean 'tie the string itself').

usage: 풀다 = work out an answer; 수학 문제를 풀다 'solve a math problem'
Idiomatic 'unwind' tension; also 피로를 풀다 'shake off fatigue'
풀다 here = undo/open up the packed bags after arriving
examples: 신발 끈 좀 풀어 줘.
Untie my shoelace for me.
Casual favor 풀어 줘; literal untie sense
이 수학 문제 같이 풀까요?
Shall we solve this math problem together?
-ㄹ까요 suggestion; 풀다 = solve, note ㄹ stays before 까
주말에 여행 가서 스트레스 좀 풀고 와요.
Go on a trip this weekend and de-stress.
스트레스를 풀다 idiom; -고 오다 'do and come back'
nuance: 풀다 covers a wide web of meanings around 'undo/release': literally to untie or unfasten (매듭을 풀다 'undo a knot'), to solve a problem (문제를 풀다), to relieve stress or fatigue (스트레스를 풀다, 피로를 풀다), to unpack (짐을 풀다), and even to blow your nose (코를 풀다). Its literal antonym is 묶다 'to tie'. Grammatically it is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ-dropping) verb: the stem ㄹ disappears before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ endings, so the formal present is 풉니다 (not 풀습니다) and the prohibitive is 풀지 마세요 — but the ㄹ stays before vowels (풀어요) and before 까 (풀까요?). The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, regularizing the irregular to 풀습니다; second, not realizing 풀다 is the everyday word for 'solve' a question — learners often hunt for a separate 'solve' verb, but 문제를 풀다 is exactly it.

Its literal antonym is 묶다 'to tie'.

Grammatically it is a ㄹ-irregular (ㄹ-dropping) verb: the stem ㄹ disappears before ㄴ, ㅂ, ㅅ endings, so the formal present is 풉니다 (not 풀습니다) and the prohibitive is 풀지 마세요 — but the ㄹ stays before vowels (풀어요) and before 까 (풀까요?).

The English-speaker pitfall is twofold: first, regularizing the irregular to 풀습니다; second, not realizing 풀다 is the everyday word for 'solve' a question — learners often hunt for a separate 'solve' verb, but 문제를 풀다 is exactly it.

mistakes: Saying 풀습니다 in formal style — 풀다 is a ㄹ-irregular, so the ㄹ drops before ㅂ: the correct form is 풉니다.
Looking for another verb to mean 'solve': for solving a problem/quiz the natural verb IS 풀다 → 문제를 풀어요, not a separate word.
Over-dropping the ㄹ before vowels: writing 푸어요 — the ㄹ only drops before ㄴ/ㅂ/ㅅ; before a vowel it stays, giving 풀어요.

usage: Everyday chore collocation; object takes 를
반으로 'into half' uses 으로 for the resulting shape/direction
종이접기 'paper folding' = origami derives from this verb
접다 = close a foldable thing; opposite 펴다/펼치다 'open out'
examples: 다 마른 빨래 좀 접어 줘.
Fold the dry laundry for me.
Casual 접어 줘; chore request between housemates
종이를 반으로 접어서 비행기를 만들어요.
Fold the paper in half and make an airplane.
-아서 'and then' links folding to the next step
비 그쳤으니까 우산 접으세요.
The rain stopped, so fold up your umbrella.
-으니까 'since' gives the reason; 접으세요 polite command
nuance: 접다 means to fold something flat — cloth, paper, an umbrella — by bending it over onto itself, and by extension to close up a foldable object. Its natural antonyms are 펴다 'to unfold/spread flat' and 펼치다 'to open out/spread wide'. Distinguish 접다 from 구기다, which is to crumple/crease messily (종이를 구기다 'crumple paper into a ball') — 접다 is neat and deliberate, 구기다 is rumpling it up. Figuratively, 접다 means to give up or fold on a plan (꿈을 접다 'give up a dream', 사업을 접다 'fold a business'), much like English 'fold'. The result/shape takes 으로: 반으로 접다 'fold in half'. The English-speaker pitfall is conjugation pronunciation — 접어요 links to [저버요] and the formal 접습니다 sounds like [접씀니다], but spelling stays 접어요/접습니다; also don't confuse neat folding (접다) with accidental crumpling (구기다).

usage: The container takes 를, the contents take 으로: 병을 물로 채우다
Same verb means 'fasten' a button or buckle — 단추를 채우다, 벨트를 채우다
Idiom for eating to satisfy hunger; 출출한 배를 채우다
examples: 물통에 물 좀 채워 줘.
Fill the water bottle for me.
Casual 채워 줘; container 물통에 takes 에
시험에서 빈칸을 다 채웠어요.
I filled in all the blanks on the test.
다 'all' + 채웠어요; form-filling sense
추우니까 단추 끝까지 채우세요.
It's cold, so button all the way up.
단추를 채우다 = fasten buttons; 끝까지 'to the end'
nuance: 채우다 is the causative 'make full' — to fill a space or container so it's no longer empty (컵에 물을 채우다). Its direct antonym is 비우다 'to empty out'. Note it's the causative partner of 차다 'to be/become full' (방이 사람으로 찼다 'the room filled with people'), so 차다 = get full on its own, 채우다 = someone fills it. A second, very common sense that surprises learners: 채우다 also means to fasten/do up a button, buckle, lock, or watch (단추를 채우다, 자물쇠를 채우다, 시계를 채우다) — here the antonym is 풀다 'undo'. And idiomatically 배를 채우다 'fill one's belly (eat)', 욕심을 채우다 'satisfy greed'. Particles: the container takes 를/에, the contents take 으로 (냉장고를 음식으로 채우다). The English-speaker pitfall is using 'fill' only for liquids/spaces and being thrown when a Korean says 단추를 채우다 — remember it doubles as 'fasten'.

usage: to spill water (a lot, at once)
Object takes 를; implies a sizable amount tipping out
The surface it lands on takes 에: 책상에 쏟았어요
Figurative 'pour out' devotion; 정성을 쏟다, 노력을 쏟다
Passive-like partner: 비가 쏟아지다 'rain pours down', 햇살이 쏟아지다
examples: 어, 커피 쏟았어!
Oops, I spilled the coffee!
Casual exclamation 쏟았어; sudden accident
아이가 우유를 식탁에 쏟았어요.
The kid spilled milk all over the table.
Surface 식탁에 takes 에; whole-amount spill
이 일에 온 정성을 쏟았어요.
I poured all my heart into this work.
정성을 쏟다 idiom; 온 'whole' intensifies
nuance: 쏟다 means to spill or pour out a sizable amount of liquid or contents all at once, usually by knocking something over — it feels stronger and more sudden than 흘리다, which is a small trickling spill (a few drops on your shirt). So 컵을 쏟다 = the whole cup goes over, 국물을 흘리다 = you dribbled a bit of broth. Figuratively 쏟다 is 'pour out' effort or emotion: 정성을 쏟다 'pour in devotion', 노력을 쏟다 'pour in effort', 눈물을 쏟다 'burst into tears'. Its intransitive/spontaneous partner is 쏟아지다 'to gush/pour down' (비가 쏟아지다 'rain pours'), so 쏟다 = someone spills it, 쏟아지다 = it pours by itself. Particles: the spilled thing takes 를, the surface it lands on takes 에 (바닥에 쏟다). The English-speaker spelling pitfall is the ㄷ batchim — write 쏟다/쏟아요 (stem 쏟-), never 쏘다요; and don't confuse it with 쏘다 'to shoot'.

usage: 치우다 = put things in order / clear away clutter; object 를
After meals you 그릇을 치우다 (clear dishes) then 설거지를 하다 (wash them)
to move ~ out of the way to ~
치우다 also = shove aside: 짐을 구석으로 치웠어요 'I moved the load to the corner'
깨끗이 'cleanly' as an adverb pairs naturally with tidying
examples: 밥 먹고 그릇 좀 치워 줘.
Clear away the dishes after eating.
Casual 치워 줘; 'clear away' sense after a meal
손님 오기 전에 방을 치웠어요.
I tidied the room before the guests came.
-기 전에 'before'; 치우다 = declutter/put in order
책상 위 좀 치우고 공부하자.
Let's clear off the desk and study.
치우다 'clear off' a surface; -고 links to the next action
nuance: 치우다 means to tidy a space by clearing things away, putting them where they belong, or moving them out of the way — the focus is on removing clutter and restoring order (방을 치우다 'tidy the room', 책상을 치우다 'clear the desk'). Contrast it with 청소하다 (Sino-Korean 淸掃, 淸 'clean' + 掃 'sweep'), which focuses on the cleaning itself — sweeping, mopping, wiping, vacuuming to remove dirt. So you 치우다 the toys (put them away) but 청소하다 the floor (mop it); a thorough clean often means doing both: 방을 치우고 청소해요. A second sense of 치우다 is simply to move/shove something out of the way (차 좀 치워 주세요 'please move your car'). The English-speaker pitfall is treating 'clean up' as one word and always saying 청소하다 — but for clearing dishes, putting away laundry, or decluttering, the right verb is 치우다. Conjugation is regular: 치우- + 어 → 치워요, past 치웠어요.
